title: Muesli
subtitle: The Bircher way, rolled oats, nuts, seeds, and dried fruit
excerpt: Muesli is a dry mix you make once and keep in a jar, ready to pour over milk, yoghurt, or juice each morning. The balance of rolled oats, nuts, seeds, and dried fruit is the key decision, everything else is just scale. Getting that right means breakfasts for the week from ten minutes of measuring.
sourceNotes: Maximilian Oskar Bircher-Benner, a Swiss physician, developed the original Bircher muesli around 1900 as a health food for his patients. His version was eaten fresh and unsoaked: grated apple, raw oats, lemon juice, condensed milk, and hazelnuts, assembled just before eating. The modern dry muesli, oats mixed with nuts, seeds, and dried fruit stored in a jar, is a simpler, longer-lasting riff on that original that became popular across Europe through the 20th century.

recipe.batchNotes: Make a larger batch, double or triple, and store in an airtight jar. Keeps at room temperature for up to 4 weeks.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Stores indefinitely in an airtight container. Make a large batch for convenience.

content.text: Muesli is the easiest breakfast in the book: measure, combine, store. There is no cooking involved, just a good ratio of {{rolled-oats}} oats to nuts, seeds, and dried fruit, mixed once and kept in a jar. Each morning you take what you need and add whatever liquid suits you: cold milk, yoghurt, juice, or warm water if you prefer it softer. The Swiss physician Maximilian Bircher-Benner invented his version around 1900 with grated apple, condensed milk, and hazelnuts eaten fresh. The dry-jar version you're making now is a later, longer-lasting adaptation, simpler, more practical, and just as good.

Tip the {{rolled-oats}} rolled oats into a large bowl. Roughly chop the {{almonds}} almonds, you want pieces, not dust, and add them to the bowl. Add the {{sunflower-seeds}} sunflower seeds, {{pumpkin-seeds}} pumpkin seeds, and {{dried-blueberries}} dried fruit. Stir everything together until evenly mixed. That is all there is to it.

Transfer to an airtight jar or container. It will keep at room temperature for up to 4 weeks, though the seeds begin to lose freshness before the oats do. If you're making a large batch, store half in the freezer and bring it out as the first jar empties.

Measure roughly 60 to 70 g per person into a bowl. The classic way is to pour over cold milk and leave it for 5 minutes to let the oats soften slightly before eating. If you prefer it much softer, soak overnight in milk, the Bircher method, and top with a grated apple and a squeeze of lemon juice in the morning. With yoghurt instead of milk you get something thicker and more filling. With apple juice rather than milk you get the lighter, fruitier Swiss version.

Bircher-Benner served his original recipe at the Vital Force sanatorium in Zurich, where he promoted raw plant foods as medicine long before that idea had much medical backing. His muesli spread through Swiss health culture and then across Europe through the 20th century. In the UK it arrived as a health food in the 1970s and 1980s, sold in health food shops in brown paper bags. It has since moved firmly into the mainstream. Every supermarket now stocks it in dozens of varieties, from lightly sweetened to loaded with chocolate. The Swiss physician would likely not approve of all of them.
Add a teaspoon of cinnamon to the dry mix for warmth.
Swap dried blueberries for dried cranberries, raisins, chopped dates, or a mix of all three.
Replace almonds with walnuts or a mixture of both, walnuts are softer and go slightly chewy after a soak.
For the true Bircher version: soak 60 g of muesli overnight in milk, then top with half a grated apple and a squeeze of lemon juice the next morning.
